summary.text: A 42-year-old man was diagnosed with moderate plaque psoriasis over 10 years ago and was initially treated with clobetasol 0.05% ointment mixed with calcipotriene 0.005% cream. His psoriasis was refractory to topicals, he was unable to attend phototherapy sessions, and a workup for systemic agents was followed by loss of follow-up because of loss of insurance. Past history included elevated transaminases from alcohol use disorder, and no personal or family history of vitiligo was recorded.

He returned in November 2022 with extensive plaque psoriasis of the trunk, upper extremities and scalp over 30% of body surface area with nail pitting and distal onycholysis. Phototherapy was not feasible and he was not a candidate for methotrexate or acitretin, and after shared decision making he started risankizumab-rzaa 150 mg subcutaneously on November 16, 2022, at 0 and 4 weeks and then every 12 weeks.

At the November 2023 follow-up his psoriasis was improved and well controlled with no active psoriasis, onycholysis or nail pitting, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and new depigmented patches described as new-onset vitiligo. He continued risankizumab-rzaa every 12 weeks plus as-needed topical triamcinolone and clobetasol, and declined vitiligo treatment because it was not bothersome.

In May 2025 he reported no active psoriasis and was tolerating risankizumab-rzaa well, with 0% body surface area involvement, residual hyperpigmented post-inflammatory patches and scattered trichrome depigmented and hypopigmented patches of active, unstable vitiligo. He continued risankizumab-rzaa every 12 weeks and opted for observation of the vitiligo; the authors regard a role for risankizumab-rzaa in the vitiligo as possible but unproven.
